name: X Pass
description: Learn the X Pass in BJJ. Comprehensive guide to executing this dynamic guard pass from half guard positions. Success rates: Beginner 45%, Intermediate 60%, Advanced 75%.
overview: The X Pass is a highly effective guard passing technique that combines pressure, angle creation, and strategic weight distribution to neutralize the bottom player's defensive structure. Originating from top half guard positions, this pass leverages crossface control and hip pressure to flatten the opponent while simultaneously clearing the legs. The technique's name derives from the cross-body angle created during execution, where the passer's torso forms an 'X' shape relative to the opponent's body. This pass is particularly effective against knee shield and standard half guard variations, as it attacks the fundamental defensive frames that bottom players rely upon. The X Pass exemplifies modern pressure passing principles by combining forward pressure with lateral movement, creating a dilemma where the opponent must choose between maintaining their guard structure or preventing the pass. When executed with proper timing and pressure application, the X Pass becomes a cornerstone technique for any guard passing system, seamlessly transitioning into dominant top positions.
key_principles: Maintain constant forward pressure throughout the pass to prevent opponent from recovering guard structure
Establish strong crossface control to flatten opponent's shoulders and eliminate defensive frames
Create angle by stepping outside leg wide while driving chest pressure across opponent's torso
Use hip pressure to pin opponent's bottom leg and prevent them from inserting butterfly hooks
Clear legs systematically by controlling the knee line and driving through any remaining frames
Transition weight smoothly from chest pressure to hip pressure as the pass completes
setup_requirements: Established top half guard position with one leg trapped between opponent's legs
Strong underhook or overhook control on the trapped side to prevent opponent from coming to their side
Opponent's defensive structure engaged (knee shield, lockdown, or standard half guard)
Crossface hand positioned to control opponent's head or neck
Base maintained on outside leg with proper weight distribution
Hip pressure applied to flatten opponent and prevent them from establishing strong frames

execution_steps.description: Drive your shoulder across opponent's face while threading your arm under their head, establishing a strong crossface. Your hand should reach toward their far shoulder or secure a grip on their far lat. This crossface serves to flatten their shoulders and eliminate their ability to frame effectively against your chest.
execution_steps.timing: Immediately upon securing top half guard position

execution_steps.description: Drive your chest weight forward and down into opponent's sternum, using your crossface shoulder as the pressure point. Your weight should be distributed approximately 70% forward onto your crossface shoulder, 30% on your base leg. This pressure prevents them from turning into you or establishing an effective underhook.

Take a wide step with your outside leg (the leg not trapped in half guard), planting your foot approximately 18-24 inches away from opponent's hip at a 45-degree angle. This creates the angle necessary for the X-shaped body position and provides a stable base for driving pressure across their body.
execution_steps.timing: As opponent reacts to initial pressure

execution_steps.description: From your wide base, drive your chest and hips diagonally across opponent's torso, moving from their near shoulder toward their far hip. Your trapped leg should begin to straighten as you drive this angle, creating space to extract. Maintain constant forward pressure while shifting your weight to follow the diagonal line.

As your angle and pressure flatten the opponent, begin extracting your trapped leg by straightening it and driving your knee toward the mat. Use your free hand to assist in controlling their bottom knee, preventing them from following your leg or re-establishing guard. Your hip pressure should pin their bottom leg to the mat as you clear.
execution_steps.timing: Once opponent is flattened and unable to maintain frames

execution_steps.description: Complete the pass by fully extracting your leg and transitioning your chest pressure into standard side control position. Your crossface should remain engaged as you settle your hip weight onto opponent's torso. Secure standard side control grips (far armpit and near hip or pants) and consolidate position before advancing.

common_counters.counter: Opponent establishes strong knee shield frame and uses it to create space and prevent forward pressure
common_counters.your_response: Address the knee shield by using your free hand to control their shin or foot, pinning it to your hip while simultaneously driving your chest pressure down into their knee. As their frame weakens, step wide and drive the angle to collapse the shield.

common_counters.counter: Opponent secures deep underhook on trapped side and uses it to come to their side and recover guard
common_counters.your_response: Prevent underhook access by maintaining tight connection with your elbow to your ribs. If underhook is established, immediately switch to over-under pass variation, using their underhook as a handle to drive them flat and complete the pass.

common_counters.counter: Opponent establishes lockdown on trapped leg and prevents leg extraction
common_counters.your_response: Address lockdown by posturing up slightly to create space, then driving your trapped knee to the mat while pulling your heel toward your glutes. This breaks the figure-four grip. Alternatively, transition to alternative passing attacks like the electric chair defense.

common_counters.counter: Opponent frames against your hips with their hands and prevents you from driving forward pressure
common_counters.your_response: Counter hip frames by using your crossface pressure to drive their shoulders flat, which naturally weakens their hip frames. Alternatively, pin one of their framing hands to their chest using your free hand, eliminating half of their defensive structure.

common_counters.counter: Opponent rolls away from you as you attempt to pass, escaping to turtle or re-establishing guard
common_counters.your_response: Follow their roll by maintaining your crossface and driving forward momentum. As they roll away, transition to back take or establish front headlock control. Never allow space to develop during their escape attempt.

common_errors.error: Rising up too high during the pass and losing chest pressure on opponent
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily establish defensive frames, re-guard, or escape to better positions. Loss of pressure eliminates your primary control mechanism.
common_errors.correction: Maintain low posture throughout the pass with constant forward pressure. Your chest should never rise more than a few inches off opponent's torso. Drive weight forward continuously.

common_errors.error: Failing to step outside leg wide enough, resulting in insufficient angle
common_errors.consequence: Pass becomes linear pressure without angle, making it easy for opponent to defend with frames and hip escapes. No X-shape is created.
common_errors.correction: Consciously step your outside leg 18-24 inches away from opponent's body at a 45-degree angle. The wider base enables the diagonal pressure line that defines this pass.

common_errors.error: Attempting to clear trapped leg too early before opponent is properly flattened
common_errors.consequence: Opponent maintains guard structure and can follow your leg with their knees, re-establishing half guard or converting to other guard positions.
common_errors.correction: Be patient with leg extraction. First flatten opponent completely with crossface and chest pressure. Only clear your leg once their defensive structure is collapsed and they cannot track your movement.

common_errors.error: Neglecting crossface control or releasing it prematurely during the pass
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can turn into you, establish underhooks, or create frames that stop your passing progression. Loss of head control equals loss of positional control.
common_errors.correction: Maintain aggressive crossface throughout entire pass sequence. Your crossface shoulder should be the last thing to release as you settle into side control. Head control is non-negotiable.

common_errors.error: Distributing weight evenly between both legs instead of loading the outside leg
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient pressure on opponent and poor base for driving angular movement. Pass becomes weak and easily defended.
common_errors.correction: Commit approximately 70% of your weight onto your outside leg and crossface shoulder. This creates maximum pressure on opponent while providing stable base for angular drives.

common_errors.error: Trying to force the pass with upper body strength alone without using hip pressure
common_errors.consequence: Pass becomes exhausting and inefficient. Opponent can maintain their guard structure through sheer defensive posture without being truly controlled.
common_errors.correction: Integrate hip pressure with chest pressure. As you drive chest forward, simultaneously drive hips forward to pin opponent's bottom leg. Use your entire body mass, not just arm and shoulder strength.

training_progressions.description: Begin with static drilling from top half guard position. Focus exclusively on establishing proper crossface, stepping to wide base, and applying chest pressure across opponent's torso. Partner remains stationary, allowing you to feel correct body positions and weight distribution. Perform 10 repetitions per side, holding final position for 5 seconds to internalize proper alignment.

training_progressions.focus: Creating the X-angle and leg clearing mechanics
training_progressions.description: Progress to drilling the complete pass sequence with emphasis on angular driving and leg extraction timing. Partner provides light resistance by maintaining guard structure but not actively defending. Practice stepping wide, driving diagonal pressure, and clearing trapped leg in smooth, continuous motion. Focus on maintaining pressure throughout entire sequence. Perform 15 repetitions per side.

Introduce specific defensive scenarios: knee shield frames, underhook attempts, and lockdown. Partner uses one defensive tactic at a time at 50% intensity. Practice appropriate responses to each counter: pinning knee shield, preventing underhooks, breaking lockdown. Cycle through 5 repetitions of each defensive scenario per side, gradually increasing resistance as success rate improves.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance implementation and position consolidation
training_progressions.description: Engage in positional sparring starting from top half guard with partner using full defensive arsenal. Practice completing X Pass against maximum resistance, troubleshooting problems as they arise. Emphasize position consolidation in side control after successful pass. 5-minute rounds, alternating positions with partner. Track success rate and identify specific defensive patterns that cause difficulty.

training_progressions.focus: Connecting X Pass to broader passing system
training_progressions.description: Practice X Pass as part of passing combinations. Set up X Pass from knee cut attempts, use it as backup when leg drag is defended, chain into other passing options when opponents defend specific aspects. Focus on reading opponent's defensive choices and selecting appropriate passing technique. Free rolling with emphasis on guard passing sequences.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Variation that incorporates over-under grips instead of standard crossface. Your crossface arm threads under opponent's far leg while your other arm wraps over their near leg, creating an over-under control structure. Drive the same angular pressure but with leg control as primary mechanism instead of crossface.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent establishes deep underhook that prevents traditional crossface, or when passing against flexible opponents who can effectively defend standard crossface pressure.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Mirror image pass executed to the opposite side, where you step your trapped leg wide instead of your free leg, creating a reverse angle. Requires different pressure mechanics but achieves same end result. Your crossface drives toward their near hip instead of far hip.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent's guard structure or grips make standard direction difficult, or when their defensive positioning naturally opens the reverse angle opportunity.

variants_and_adaptations.variant_name: X Pass to Knee on Belly
variants_and_adaptations.description: High-level variation where instead of settling in side control, you continue your angular momentum to transition directly into knee on belly position. Requires excellent balance and timing but provides immediate dominant pressure position.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against opponents who effectively defend side control consolidation or when competing under rulesets that reward dominant position advancement quickly.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why is stepping the outside leg wide at a 45-degree angle critical to the X Pass execution?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Stepping wide creates the angular pressure line that defines the X Pass and distinguishes it from linear pressure passing. The wide base allows you to drive your chest and hips diagonally across opponent's torso rather than straight forward. This angle makes it significantly harder for the opponent to frame effectively because their defensive frames would need to extend at awkward angles to meet your pressure. Additionally, the wide base provides stability for maintaining pressure while clearing your trapped leg.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the relationship between crossface control and successful leg clearing during the X Pass?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The crossface serves to flatten opponent's shoulders to the mat, which cascades into flattening their entire defensive structure. When their shoulders are flat, they cannot effectively turn into you, establish strong frames, or track your leg as you extract it. The crossface essentially immobilizes their upper body, which makes controlling their lower body and clearing your trapped leg significantly easier. Without proper crossface, the opponent can turn their shoulders and hips to follow your leg movement, preventing the pass.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you distribute your body weight during the X Pass and why?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Approximately 70% of your weight should be loaded onto your outside leg and crossface shoulder, with 30% on your base leg. This distribution maximizes pressure on the opponent while maintaining a stable base for angular movement. The heavy forward load onto the crossface creates the flattening pressure that collapses their defensive structure, while the strong outside base provides the platform for driving diagonal pressure across their body. Even weight distribution would reduce pressure effectiveness and compromise your ability to generate angle.

knowledge_assessment.question: What should you do if your opponent establishes a strong knee shield frame that prevents your forward pressure?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Address the knee shield by using your free hand to control their shin or foot, pinning it to your hip to prevent them from extending the frame. Simultaneously drive chest pressure down into the top of their knee rather than trying to pressure through it. As their frame weakens under this downward pressure, immediately step wide and drive your angle to collapse the shield completely. The key is attacking the knee shield's base (the foot) while applying pressure to its structure (the knee), rather than trying to overpower it with linear force.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why is it important to be patient with leg extraction and wait until the opponent is fully flattened?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Attempting to clear your trapped leg before the opponent is properly flattened allows them to track your leg movement with their knees and hips, re-establishing half guard or transitioning to other guard positions. When the opponent is fully flattened with effective crossface and pressure, their ability to move their lower body is severely compromised. Their flattened structure prevents them from generating the hip movement necessary to follow your leg. Rushing the leg clear before establishing positional dominance is one of the most common reasons the X Pass fails at high levels.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the X Pass create a dilemma for the bottom player?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The X Pass creates a fundamental dilemma because the angular pressure forces the bottom player to choose between multiple defensive priorities simultaneously. They must choose between: maintaining their guard structure (keeping their knees together), defending the crossface (preventing their shoulders from being flattened), or framing against the hip pressure (stopping the passer's weight from settling). Defending one aspect typically weakens another. If they focus on the crossface, their guard structure weakens. If they maintain their guard, they cannot effectively frame. This multi-directional threat is what makes the X Pass highly effective against sophisticated guard players.

safety_considerations: The X Pass is generally a safe passing technique when executed with proper control and awareness. The primary safety concern is maintaining control of your weight distribution to avoid dropping knee or elbow pressure onto opponent's ribs or floating ribs, which can cause injury. When driving crossface pressure, be mindful of neck positioning and avoid cranking the neck at extreme angles. Apply pressure gradually rather than explosively, especially when training with less experienced partners. If opponent signals discomfort or taps due to pressure (particularly rib or neck pressure), immediately release and adjust your positioning. During drilling phases, communicate with your partner about pressure levels and adjust according to their feedback. When clearing your trapped leg, avoid forcefully kicking or pushing off opponent's legs, which can hyperextend their knee or ankle joints.
position_integration: The X Pass represents a cornerstone technique in modern pressure passing systems, serving as both a primary attack and a backup option when other passes are defended. It integrates seamlessly into systematic guard passing progressions, particularly excelling as a follow-up when knee cut passes or leg drag attempts are defended with strong frames or underhooks. The pass is particularly valuable in half guard top positions, where it provides a reliable pathway from challenging guard retention positions to dominant top control. Within a complete passing system, the X Pass chains effectively with smash passing variations, over-under passes, and knee through sequences, creating a pressure-based passing network that addresses multiple defensive scenarios. The technique also serves as an entry point for back takes when opponents attempt to escape by turning away, and naturally transitions to knee on belly or mount when opponents defend the side control consolidation. For no-gi grapplers, the X Pass becomes even more critical as it relies primarily on weight distribution and body positioning rather than gi grips, making it a universal technique across ruleset variations.
